passages.title: The City After the Commute
passages.body:
**A**  In 2020, millions of office workers were sent home within a few weeks. What was meant to be a temporary arrangement became, for many companies, a permanent option. Employees saved the time and money they had spent travelling, and some moved to smaller towns where housing was cheaper. By 2023, office occupancy in several large cities was still well below its pre-2020 level, and landlords were offering shorter leases to attract tenants.

**B**  The benefits are easy to see. Workers gain flexibility and avoid the daily commute; employers can recruit from a wider area and spend less on desks. Smaller firms that could never afford an office in a capital city can now compete for the same staff. For parents and people with disabilities, remote work has removed barriers that office attendance had kept in place.

**C**  The costs fall unevenly. City centres that depended on office workers have lost customers: sandwich shops, dry cleaners and bus operators all report lower takings. Junior employees lose the informal learning that happens when they sit near experienced colleagues. And the freedom to work from home is not shared equally: builders, nurses and shop staff cannot do their jobs on a laptop, so the benefits tend to flow to professional workers.

**D**  Most predictions now point to a hybrid future rather than the end of the office. Companies bring teams together for a few days a week and allow quiet work at home on others. Cities are adjusting too, converting empty offices into flats and rethinking transport schedules that were designed around the five-day commute. The office is unlikely to disappear, but it is becoming a place people visit rather than a place they occupy.

questions.prompt: Remote work has reduced the time many people spend commuting.
questions.explanation: Paragraph A: employees saved the time they had spent travelling.

questions.prompt: Every kind of job can be done remotely.
questions.explanation: Paragraph C says builders, nurses and shop staff cannot do their jobs on a laptop.

questions.prompt: City centres have been unaffected by the shift to remote work.
questions.explanation: Paragraph C describes lost customers for shops and bus operators.

questions.prompt: The writer expects offices to disappear completely.
questions.explanation: Paragraph D says the office is unlikely to disappear.

questions.prompt: What advantage do employers gain from remote work?
options: They can recruit from a wider area.
questions.explanation: Paragraph B: employers can recruit from a wider area.

questions.prompt: What problem does remote work create for city centres?
questions.explanation: Paragraph C: shops and transport operators report lower takings.

questions.prompt: What does the writer suggest about hybrid work?
options: It is likely to remain common.
questions.explanation: Paragraph D: most predictions point to a hybrid future.

questions.prompt: Junior staff may miss the informal learning that happens near experienced ______.

questions.explanation: Paragraph A describes the rapid shift to home working in 2020.
